blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The book prints only the heading here and goes straight on to 8.5.1. This short introduction is ours.
So far the binomial theorem has been used to expand \((a + b)^{n}\). Section 8.5 uses it as a tool for whole numbers: to find the remainder when a large power is divided by a number, to find the last digit or last two digits of a large power, and to prove that an expression is divisible by a number.
The one idea behind all of them: write the base as (a multiple of the divisor) \(\pm\) (a small number), for example \(8 = 7 + 1\) or \(2 = 3 - 1\). When the power is expanded, every term except the last contains the divisor, so only the last term decides the answer. Powers such as \(8^{100}\) are far too large to work out, yet this method needs only a few lines.
